message.content:
Let  
\[
p(n)=n^2-n+41
\]
and  
\[
p(n+1)=(n+1)^2-(n+1)+41=n^2+n+41.
\]

Suppose \(p(n)\) and \(p(n+1)\) have a common factor \(d>1\). Then \(d\) divides their difference:
\[
p(n+1)-p(n)=(n^2+n+41)-(n^2-n+41)=2n.
\]
So every prime factor of \(d\) divides \(2n\).

Now,
\[
p(n)=n^2-n+41=n(n-1)+41
\]
is always odd, so \(2\) cannot be a common factor. Thus any common prime factor \(q\) is odd, and since \(q\mid 2n\), we must have \(q\mid n\).

If \(q\mid n\), then
\[
p(n)=n^2-n+41\equiv 41 \pmod q.
\]
For \(q\) to divide \(p(n)\), we need \(q\mid 41\). Since \(41\) is prime, \(q=41\).

Therefore, a common factor greater than \(1\) can occur only when \(41\mid n\). The smallest positive such \(n\) is
\[
n=41.
\]

Check:
\[
p(41)=41^2-41+41=41^2=1681,
\]
\[
p(42)=42^2-42+41=1763=41\cdot 43.
\]
They share the common factor \(41\).

The answer is 41.
